caveats: Trends are straight-line summaries of annual averages. They cannot capture cycles, sudden jumps or curved change.
NASA POWER blends satellite observations with computer models (reanalysis) on a grid about half a degree wide, so points that are close together can share the same values.
A significant trend shows a consistent direction over this period, not its cause. A different start or end year can change the answer.

verdict.label: Strong evidence of a trend
verdict.summary: Air temperature at (33.45, -112.07) rose over 1981–2024: +0.624 °C per decade (95% range +0.581 to +0.657), about +2.68 °C in total. That change is roughly 17.6× the normal year-to-year swing. Strong evidence (5 of 5 checks passed).

completeness.source: NASA Langley Research Center (LaRC) POWER Project

slope_and_interval.method: Theil–Sen median pairwise slope with Gilbert (1987) 95% confidence interval

mann_kendall.method: Two-sided Mann–Kendall non-parametric trend test (tie- and continuity-corrected)

serial_correlation.method: Marriott–Pope (1954) bias-corrected lag-1 autocorrelation variance inflation (1+phi)/(1-phi)

correction_status.explanation: A single requested point trend is tested at alpha = 0.05 using the serial-correlation-adjusted p-value. Simultaneous families of tests (the 12 calendar months here, plus Sweep, Scan, World, and Ledger) apply Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery control at q = 0.05.

steps.title: Count complete 12-month years
steps.plain_explanation: Used 44 complete 12-month years (1981–2024) from 528 valid monthly observations so no single season biases the annual average.
steps.method_label: Complete-year annual aggregation (12 valid months required per year)

steps.title: Estimate rate of change (Theil–Sen slope & 95% interval)
steps.plain_explanation: Compared every pair of years to find the median rate of change: +0.624 °C/decade (95% interval +0.581 to +0.657 °C/decade).
steps.method_label: Theil–Sen estimator with Gilbert (1987) 95% confidence interval

steps.title: Check whether neighboring years resemble each other
steps.plain_explanation: Measured year-to-year persistence (lag-1 autocorrelation r1 = -0.07) and applied a variance factor of 1.00× (no material persistence widening needed).

steps.title: Run non-parametric and regression significance tests
steps.plain_explanation: Mann–Kendall p = < 0.001 (raw unadjusted p = < 0.001) and OLS regression t-test p = < 0.001 with 42.0 effective degrees of freedom.
steps.method_label: Tie-corrected Mann–Kendall test + effective-df Student-t OLS regression

steps.title: Combine five robustness checks into the evidence verdict
steps.plain_explanation: Passed 5 of 5 evidence checks → Strong evidence of a trend.
steps.method_label: Five-check evidence rubric + Benjamini–Hochberg FDR on calendar months

explanations_ok.summary: Possible explanations, not proof of cause. The Arctic is warming roughly two to four times faster than the planet. Melting sea ice and snow expose darker surfaces that soak up more sunlight, which amplifies the warming ('Arctic amplification').
explanations_ok.disclaimer: These are possible explanations, not proof that one cause created this local trend.

drivers.title: Measured local air temperature trend
drivers.explanation: Across 44 complete years (1981–2024), air temperature moved +0.585 °C per decade (Mann–Kendall p = 6.27e-18). This establishes what changed, not what caused it.
